title: What is the var keyword in Java, where can and cannot it be used, and why is the variable still statically typed?
shortTitle: What is the var keyword in Java?
keyPoints: var is local variable type inference, introduced in Java 10 – the compiler infers the type from the initializer
The variable is still statically typed at compile time – var is NOT dynamic typing like JavaScript or Python
Allowed for: local variables with initializer, for-loop index, for-each element, try-with-resources
NOT allowed for: fields, method parameters, return types, catch parameters, or var x = null
The generated bytecode is identical to writing the explicit type – zero runtime cost
Use var when the right-hand side makes the type obvious; keep explicit types when it aids readability

s1_definition.oneliner: var lets the compiler infer a local variable's type from its initializer at compile time. It is shorthand for the full type, not dynamic typing.
s1_definition.profdef:
Three facts define var:

- **Inference, not magic.** When you write `var account = new Account("SAV2001")`, the compiler reads the right-hand side and substitutes `Account` as the type. The bytecode is identical to writing `Account account = new Account("SAV2001")`.
- **Local only.** var works for local variables, for-loop variables, for-each variables, and try-with-resources variables. It does not work for fields, parameters, or return types.
- **Still static.** The type is fixed at compile time. You cannot later assign an incompatible type. This is type inference, not dynamic typing.
s1_definition.analogy: When you fill a bank form, instead of writing "Savings Account" in the account type box, you attach the passbook and let the clerk read the type from it. The clerk stamps the exact type permanently. If you attach a savings passbook, the form is stamped "Savings" forever. You cannot later swap in a loan document. The clerk also refuses to stamp if you attach nothing. That is var: the compiler reads the type from what you assign, stamps it permanently, and refuses if there is nothing to read from.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  ── var: compile-time inference flow ──

  Source code:   var account = new Account("SAV2001");
                      │
                      │ compiler reads RHS type
                      ▼
  Inferred type: Account account = new Account("SAV2001");
                      │
                      │ javac emits bytecode
                      ▼
  Bytecode:      identical to explicit Account declaration
                 (no runtime difference, no overhead)


  ── Where var is allowed ──

  var x = expr;             local with initializer       ✓
  for (var i = 0; ...)      for-loop index               ✓
  for (var e : list)        for-each element              ✓
  try (var r = open())      try-with-resources            ✓

  ── Where var is NOT allowed ──

  class field               part of type contract         ✗
  method parameter          part of signature contract    ✗
  return type               part of signature contract    ✗
  catch parameter           must be explicit              ✗
  var x;                    no initializer to infer from  ✗
  var x = null;             null has no specific type     ✗


  ── var vs dynamic typing ──

  Java:       var s = "hi"; s = 42;     → COMPILE ERROR (static)
  JavaScript: let s = "hi"; s = 42;     → OK (dynamic)
  Python:     s = "hi"; s = 42          → OK (dynamic)
  Kotlin:     var s = "hi"; s = 42      → COMPILE ERROR (static, like Java)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
var, introduced in Java 10, is local variable type inference. When you write `var account = new Account("SAV2001")`, the compiler reads the right-hand side, infers the type as `Account`, and substitutes it. The bytecode is identical to writing the explicit type. There is zero runtime cost.

var is allowed in four places: local variables with an initializer, for-loop index variables, for-each loop elements, and try-with-resources variables. It is not allowed on fields, method parameters, return types, or catch parameters, because those are part of a type contract that must be explicit. It also cannot be used without an initializer or with null, because the compiler has nothing to infer from.

The most important thing to remember is that var is not dynamic typing. The type is fixed at compile time and never changes. If var infers `String`, you cannot later assign an `int`. This is fundamentally different from JavaScript or Python, where a variable can hold any type. Java's var is type inference, not type flexibility.

In our banking codebase, var cleans up verbose declarations like `Map<String, List<BigDecimal>>` where the constructor already states the type. But we keep explicit types on fields and method signatures because those are contracts, and we keep explicit types on locals where the right-hand side is a method call with an unclear return type. We also always write the type argument on the right of the diamond when using var, because `var list = new ArrayList<>()` infers `ArrayList<Object>`, which is almost never what you want.

One sentence to remember: var infers a local variable's type from its initializer at compile time, produces identical bytecode, and is still fully statically typed.
